Goal / Input / Constraints
* Please format "X" as a {{constant}} and remove the quotation marks.

Constraints
* Please change both "{{cell}}" and "cell" to "cell value" (unformatted).

Input
* Please change:

"A list of length n, each list item is a string representing"

to:

"[[n]] space-separated values representing the cells in each row. Each value is either".

Stub generator
* Please change 50 to 2.

Goal
* "Cells that share an axis with both placed pieces" sounds incorrect to me, at least in the case where the pieces are in different rows and columns. In such a case, each candidate cell shares a row with one piece and a column with the other. So, please correct the wording.

* Your comment states "the two points are in the same row or column, in which case, either the highest priority available cell or the highest priority cell between the two pieces is chosen." What if the two pieces are next to each other? There would be no cell between the two pieces.

* Still on the same row/column scenario: there may not be exactly two candidate cells as claimed in the first paragraph of the statement; there may be fewer or more.

Cases
* "The options are (a single digit number n) and (a number < n*10)" is a good idea. Please implement it.

* The current cases appear to be paired based only on grid size (n) only. 

  Assuming
  • The Xs are at (x1, y1) and (x2, y2)
  • y2 > y1
  • Let dx = x2 - x1 and dy = y2 - y1. 
  
  Ignoring same-row and same-column cases, for more systematic and balanced coverage, consider revising the pairing so that each pair shares:

  • the same value of n,

  • the same sign of dx (dx > 0 or dx < 0), and

  • the same relative displacement category:
    - abs(dx) = abs(dy)
    - abs(dx) > abs(dy)
    - abs(dx) < abs(dy)

Thanks.

I've just noticed that all of the tests can be passed without converting the input to an integer. I don't necessarily think that's a problem, probably a cool easter egg for shortest mode, but I can fix it with testcases where the options are (a single digit number n) and (a number < n*10). 
Upvote this comment if I should implement those cases.

I am considering including test cases where the two points are in the same row or column, in which case, either the highest priority available cell or the highest priority cell between the two pieces is chosen. 
So long as it doesn't make the puzzle too difficult for a clash, I would like to change the task to: print the board after placing the new piece in the best position.
I am also considering making another version of this for reverse (and maybe shortest mode) where the board is always size 3.
Opinions on any topic would be appreciated.

That was quick.

For the notes on the idea in my comment, I hadn't planned on a test case where they're right next to each other, but that's a good idea. As such, if I were to proceed with that plan, the selection would have to be made from all cells in the grid, which makes sense since you no longer get the benefit of blocking the opponent and extending your line. I could probably take it further and say in that case, find the highest value cell in the row/column that the opponent does not share, so as to extend the line, but I would then have to change the pieces to be player specific, and I also don't want to make it too hard for the average clasher.

For the validator pairing, the first four are basically the test case but rotated, the last four are somewhat random but not entirely. Assuming I understand your suggestion, it would be good to implement. Basically, you're saying the pieces should maintain their relative direction (ie. top piece stays to the left/right of bottom piece in both tests)?

1. I'd go with the latter wording. I think it's easier to understand, especially for non-native speakers.

2. Having more scenarios (same row / same column / adjacent cells) would add a bit of complexity as you've described. By the way, if you decide *not* to include same-row/column cases, remember to make that explicit in the Constraints section.

3. Yes, that's what I meant for the case pairing: maintain the relative direction of the pieces and their relative displacement (note) in each pair of cases.

Note: It's sufficient that the (in)equality between abs(dx) and abs(dy) to be the same in each pair; the actual values can still differ between the test and the validator. For example, if they're equal, the test could have dx = dy = 3, while the validator has dx = dy = 2.

By the way, please do *not* format "cell" as a {{constant}} in the Constraints section, as it's not a constant.
